Numerical Methods, Lecture 5: lecture, seminar and lab

Press the same key until the answer stops changing.

That is how many equations with no closed-form solution get solved: start from an approximation and improve it, step by step. Drag the pink point and watch the sequence close in on the solution.

Here you learn why this works, when it works, how fast it works and how to program it.

How to use this material

This material fully covers the learning unit "Lecture 5" (4. The method of successive approximations on R and 5. Newton's method on R. The tangent method). Read it from top to bottom: each section builds on the one before. The four dots next to each title show its level.

BeginnerYou understand the ideas from pictures and examples, without heavy proofs.
IntermediateYou apply the theorems and solve exam-style exercises on your own.
AdvancedYou prove the results and write robust programs.
Top performanceYou understand the limits of the methods, the order of convergence and acceleration.
If…Go through
this is your first time with the subjectP1–P3, then A1–A5 and B1–B3, with all the interactive modules; come back to the proofs later

Unit objectives

The source document has no explicit list of objectives. I derived them from its content, and at the end of this material (Z2) a matrix links each element of the source to the section that covers it.

By the end you will be able to:

  1. define and recognize fixed points and α-contractions, geometrically and analytically;
  2. prove the uniqueness of the fixed point, the derivative criterion and the existence of a fixed point;
  3. turn f(x)=0 into x=g(x) and check the hypotheses of the fixed-point theorem;
  4. compute the number of iterations for a given accuracy and choose a stopping criterion;
  5. derive Newton's formula and use its error estimates;
  6. choose x0​ correctly with the tangent theorem and recognize failure situations;
  7. implement, test and compare the methods in a program.

Before you start

Three short refreshers. If you already know them, go straight to A1.

P1 What solving an equation numerically means beginner

The equation x2=4 has an exact answer. The equation cosx=x has no formula that gives its solution. Polynomial equations of degree 5 or higher cannot, in general, be solved by radicals either. Still, the solutions exist, and in practice we need them to a certain number of decimals.

An iterative method produces a sequence of approximations x0​,x1​,x2​,… that approaches the solution. We need three answers:

  • Convergence: does the sequence surely approach the solution?
  • Speed: how many steps are needed?
  • Stopping: how do we know we can stop?

For the absolute error we use ∣xn​−ξ∣, where ξ (read "xi") is the exact solution. Saying "with an error ≤10−4" means ∣xn​−ξ∣≤0.0001. Since the solution is unknown, the error has to be estimated, not computed. This is where the theorems of this lecture come in.

P2 Three calculus theorems you need beginner

The intermediate value theorem

A continuous function cannot go from negative to positive values without passing through 0. If f is continuous on [a,b] and f(a)⋅f(b)≤0, there exists ξ∈[a,b] with f(ξ)=0.

Example. For f(x)=x2−2 we have f(1)=−1<0 and f(2)=2>0, so there is a root in [1,2]. It is 2​.

Lagrange's theorem (the mean value theorem)

If g is continuous on [x,y] and differentiable on (x,y), there is a point c between x and y where the tangent is parallel to the chord:

g(y)−g(x)=g′(c)(y−x).

Example. If we know that ∣g′∣≤21​ everywhere, then ∣g(y)−g(x)∣≤21​∣y−x∣: a small derivative means distances shrink. This is the central link of the lecture.

Taylor's formula of order 2

Near the point a, a function looks like its tangent, plus a correction:

f(x)=f(a)+f′(a)(x−a)+2f′′(c)​(x−a)2,c between a and x.

The first two terms are exactly the equation of the tangent. Newton starts from here.

P3 Rolle's sequence: how many roots are there? intermediate

The source uses the phrase "using Rolle's sequence" without details. The method says: between two consecutive zeros of the derivative, the function has at most one root, because it is monotonic on that interval.

  1. Compute f′ and find its zeros c1​<c2​<⋯<ck​.
  2. Build the table of values of f at −∞,c1​,…,ck​,+∞ (limits at the ends).
  3. Each sign change between two consecutive positions indicates exactly one root in that interval.
Example 1: f(x)=x3+12x−1, from the lecture

f′(x)=3x2+12>0 everywhere: the derivative has no zeros, so f is strictly increasing.

x−∞+∞
sign of f−+

One sign change, so one real root. Since f(0)=−1<0 and f(1)=12>0, it lies in [0,1].

Example 2: f(x)=x3−3x+1

f′(x)=3x2−3=0 gives c1​=−1, c2​=1. The values: f(−1)=3, f(1)=−1.

x−∞−11+∞
sign of f−+−+

Three sign changes, so three real roots: one in each of the intervals (−∞,−1), (−1,1) and (1,+∞).

Remember

Before any numerical method, isolate the roots: find how many there are and, for each one, an interval containing only that root. All the theorems of this lecture assume you have already done this.

Lecture: successive approximations

The simplest idea: rewrite the equation as x=g(x) and repeat xn+1​=g(xn​).

A1 The COS key experiment beginner

Take a scientific calculator set to radians. Enter any number and press the COS key, again and again. Try it here:

Whatever the start, you reach the same number: 0.7390851… Without knowing it, the calculator has solved the equation cosx=x.

Why? If the sequence xn+1​=cosxn​ has the limit L, passing to the limit in this relation (cosine being continuous) gives L=cosL. The limit, if it exists, is a solution of the equation. What remains is to know when the limit exists. That is the subject of this entire part.

A useful picture

Hold a map of the city above the city. Exactly one point on the map lies directly above the place it represents. The map "shrinks" distances, and a fixed point is guaranteed. This is, in essence, the theorem we are going to prove.

A2 Fixed point beginner

Definition 1 (fixed point)

Let g:[a,b]→R. A point p∈[a,b] is called a fixed point of g if g(p)=p.

In other words, g does not move p. Three numerical examples:

  • g(x)=x2: g(0)=0 and g(1)=1, so 0 and 1 are fixed points. However, g(2)=4=2.
  • g(x)=2x​+1: solving 2x​+1=x gives p=2. Check: g(2)=2.
  • g(x)=x+1: the equation x+1=x has no solutions, so there are no fixed points.

The geometric picture (Remark 3 in the source)

The condition g(p)=p says that the point (p,p) lies on the graph of g and on the first bisector y=x. So: a real root of the equation x=g(x) is the abscissa of the intersection point of the curve y=g(x) and the line y=x.

How many fixed points does the function have?

The dashed pink line is y = x. The fixed points are the intersections.

Which is a fixed point of g(x)=x2−2x?

  1. x=2
  2. x=3
  3. x=1

A3 Contractions: functions that bring points closer beginner

Definition 2 (α-contraction)

The function g is called an α-contraction on [a,b] if there exists α∈(0,1) such that ∣g(x)−g(y)∣≤α⋅∣x−y∣,∀x,y∈[a,b].

Read the inequality as follows: any two points, after applying g, end up closer, by at least the factor α. What matters is that the constant is the same for all pairs.

Complete example. g(x)=2x​+1. Take x=0, y=2: g(0)=1, g(2)=2. The distance was 2 and became 1, so the ratio is 21​. In general: ∣g(x)−g(y)∣=​2x​−2y​​=21​∣x−y∣, so g is a 21​-contraction.

Measure the shrinking ratio

The pink segment is the distance between x and y. The green segment is the distance between their images. Move the sliders and watch the ratio, especially for the functions that are not contractions.

Common mistake

It is not enough for the ratio to be less than 1 for each pair. For sinx on [0,1.5], the ratio is always below 1, but it gets arbitrarily close to 1 near 0. No α<1 works for all pairs. See the module above, last function.

A4 Three fundamental remarks, with proofs intermediate

Remark 2: a small derivative guarantees contraction

Checking the definition on all pairs is hard. The derivative makes it easy, which is why we discuss it first.

Remark 2

If g:[a,b]→R is differentiable and there exists α∈(0,1) such that ∣g′(x)∣≤α for every x∈[a,b], then g is an α-contraction.

  1. Let x,y∈[a,b], with x<y (if x=y, the inequality is obvious). Being differentiable, g is continuous on [x,y].
  2. Apply Lagrange's theorem on [x,y]: there is c∈(x,y) with g(y)−g(x)=g′(c)(y−x).
  3. Take absolute values: ∣g(x)−g(y)∣=∣g′(c)∣⋅∣x−y∣.
  4. By hypothesis, ∣g′(c)∣≤α, so ∣g(x)−g(y)∣≤α∣x−y∣. This is exactly the definition. ∎

Example. g(x)=cosx on [0,1]: ∣g′(x)∣=sinx≤sin1≈0.8415<1. So g is a contraction with α=sin1.

Remark 1: at most one fixed point

Remark 1

If g is an α-contraction and has a fixed point, then that point is unique.

  1. Suppose there are two fixed points, p1​ and p2​: g(p1​)=p1​, g(p2​)=p2​.
  2. From the definition of a contraction: ∣g(p1​)−g(p2​)∣≤α∣p1​−p2​∣. Replace g(pi​) with pi​ on the left-hand side.
  3. We get ∣p1​−p2​∣≤α∣p1​−p2​∣, that is ∣p1​−p2​∣(1−α)≤0.
  4. Since 1−α>0, it follows that ∣p1​−p2​∣≤0, so p1​=p2​. ∎ Intuitively: the distance between two fixed points does not change, but a contraction would have to shrink it. The only possibility is distance zero.

Remark 3: existence of a fixed point

Remark 3

If g:[a,b]→[a,b] is continuous, then g has a fixed point.

Note the codomain [a,b]: the graph stays inside the square [a,b]×[a,b]. If it starts on the left side and reaches the right side, it must cross the diagonal. No contraction is required here.

  1. Define h:[a,b]→R, h(x)=g(x)−x. The function h is continuous.
  2. Since g(a)∈[a,b], we have g(a)≥a, so h(a)=g(a)−a≥0.
  3. Since g(b)∈[a,b], we have g(b)≤b, so h(b)=g(b)−b≤0.
  4. So h(a)⋅h(b)≤0 and, h being continuous, there is p∈[a,b] with h(p)=0, that is g(p)=p. ∎
How they connect

Remark 3 gives existence, Remark 1 gives uniqueness, Remark 2 gives a practical test for contraction. Together, they lead to the theorem in A5.

A5 The theorem of successive approximations intermediate

Theorem (method of successive approximations)

Let g:[a,b]→[a,b] be an α-contraction, with α∈(0,1). Then, for every x0​∈[a,b], the sequence (xn​)n∈N​ given by xn+1​=g(xn​),∀n∈N, converges to the unique fixed point p of g. Moreover, the following estimate holds: ∣xn​−p∣≤αn(b−a),∀n∈N∗.

The cobweb diagram

The iteration has a simple picture that you can construct with a ruler:

  1. Start from x0​ on the Ox axis and go vertically up to the curve y=g(x). You are now at height g(x0​)=x1​.
  2. Go horizontally to the bisector y=x. The abscissa is now x1​.
  3. Repeat.
The iteration lab

Press "Next step" and watch the table. Drag the pink point or move the slider for another x₀. Try the last three functions: they show what happens when the hypotheses fail.

Positive slope, 0<g′(p)<1

The diagram looks like a staircase: the sequence approaches from one side, monotonically. Try x+2​.

Negative slope, −1<g′(p)<0

The diagram looks like a spiral: the sequence jumps alternately to either side of p. Try cosx.

The proof

The source states the theorem without proof, but refers to it ("from the proof of Banach's theorem"). Here it is in full.

  1. The sequence is well defined. Since g maps [a,b] into [a,b], all terms xn​ stay in [a,b] and g can always be applied.
  2. The fixed point exists and is unique. A contraction is continuous: if xk​→x, then ∣g(xk​)−g(x)∣≤α∣xk​−x∣→0. Remark 3 gives the existence of p, and Remark 1 gives uniqueness.
  3. One step brings us closer by the factor α. ∣xn​−p∣=∣g(xn−1​)−g(p)∣≤α∣xn−1​−p∣. We use p=g(p) and the definition of a contraction.
  4. Iterate the inequality. ∣xn​−p∣≤α∣xn−1​−p∣≤α2∣xn−2​−p∣≤⋯≤αn∣x0​−p∣.
  5. Bound the initial distance. x0​ and p are in [a,b], so ∣x0​−p∣≤b−a. Thus ∣xn​−p∣≤αn(b−a).
  6. Convergence. Since 0<α<1, we have αn→0. So ∣xn​−p∣→0, that is xn​→p. ∎

Speed depends on α (Remark 4)

The smaller α is, the faster the convergence. The error decreases like a geometric progression.

How much α matters

On the vertical axis, each division means 100 times smaller. A straight line on this chart means geometric decrease.

A6 How close are we? Error estimates intermediate

The source gives two a priori bounds (computable before iterating). We add a third, a posteriori bound (computed during the iteration), which is very useful in practice.

The estimateWhat you need to knowType
∣xn​−p∣≤αn(b−a)α, a, ba priori (the theorem)
∣xn​−p∣≤1−ααn​∣x0​−x1​∣α, the first stepa priori (Remark 7)
∣xn​−p∣≤1−αα​∣xn​−xn−1​∣α, the last stepa posteriori (addition)

Proof of the estimate in Remark 7

  1. Steps shrink geometrically. ∣xk+1​−xk​∣=∣g(xk​)−g(xk−1​)∣≤α∣xk​−xk−1​∣, so ∣xk+1​−xk​∣≤αk∣x1​−x0​∣.
  2. Distance over several steps. With the triangle inequality, for m>n: ∣xm​−xn​∣≤k=n∑m−1​∣xk+1​−xk​∣≤∣x1​−x0​∣k=n∑m−1​αk.
  3. Bound with the geometric series. ∑k=n∞​αk=1−ααn​, so ∣xm​−xn​∣≤1−ααn​∣x1​−x0​∣.
  4. Pass to the limit. For m→∞, xm​→p and we get ∣p−xn​∣≤1−ααn​∣x0​−x1​∣. ∎

The a posteriori estimate follows by applying the same result with n=1, taking xn−1​ as the new starting point: ∣xn​−p∣≤1−αα​∣xn−1​−xn​∣.

The bounds compared with the real error

The lines of the bounds stay above the real error. When they are far above it, the theorem asks for more iterations than were actually needed.

How to find the number of iterations

You want 1−ααn​∣x1​−x0​∣<ε. Taking logarithms (careful, lnα<0 flips the inequality):

n>lnαln∣x1​−x0​∣ε(1−α)​​.

For example, for cosx on [0,1], with x0​=0, α=sin1, ∣x1​−x0​∣=1, ε=10−3, the formula gives n≥51. The table below shows that the real error drops below 10−3 already at n=16: the bound is a guarantee, not a forecast.

A7 From f(x) = 0 to x = g(x) intermediate

The theorem is about x=g(x), but we usually have f(x)=0. We must rewrite the equation (Remark 2 in the source). An equation allows many rewritings, and not all of them work.

Take x5+x3−16=0, which has the unique root ξ≈1.6337 in [1,2]:

The rewriting x=g(x)How we got it∣g′(ξ)∣Result
x=516−x3​isolate x5≈ 0.22fast
x=31+x216​​x3(x2+1)=16≈ 0.48slower
x=x4+x216​x(x4+x2)=16≈ 3.5diverges
x=316−x5​isolate x3≈ 4.4diverges
The same equation, four rewritings

All have the same root, that is, the same intersection with y = x. What differs is the slope of the curve at that point.

The complete checking recipe

  1. Interval: find [a,b] containing a single root (Rolle's sequence, signs).
  2. Rewriting: write x=g(x), aiming for g to have a small slope near the root.
  3. Contraction: compute α=sup[a,b]​∣g′(x)∣ and check α<1.
  4. Invariance: check g([a,b])⊆[a,b]. If g is monotonic, comparing g(a) and g(b) with a and b is enough.
  5. Iterations: choose x0​, compute x1​ and determine n from the estimate.
Addition to the source

Remark 2 in the source mentions g:[a,b]→R with ∣g′∣≤α<1. To apply the theorem, the condition g([a,b])⊆[a,b] is also needed. Counterexample: g(x)=2x​+3 on [0,1] has ∣g′∣=21​, but its fixed point is 6, outside the interval; a sequence started in [0,1] leaves the interval immediately.

A8 Stopping, refinement and hypotheses advanced

When to stop (Remarks 5 and 6)

The iterative process continues until:

∣xn+1​−xn​∣≤εor∣f(xn​)∣≤ε.

If xn​=0, the relative error can be used instead of the absolute error:

​1−xn​xn+1​​​≤ε.

The relative error is suitable when solutions are very large or very small: an absolute ε=10−3 says nothing about a solution of the order of 10−6.

In addition, always limit the number of iterations to some nmax​. If you reach the limit without meeting the criterion, treat the situation as possible divergence, instead of getting stuck forever.

The trap of practical criteria

The last column is the real error. Compare it with ε.

Important

A small step does not guarantee a small error, and a small value of ∣f∣ does not guarantee closeness to the root. If you know α, the correct guarantee is 1−αα​∣xn​−xn−1​∣≤ε. When α is close to 1, the factor 1−αα​ becomes very large.

Refining approximations (Remark 1)

The method can be used to refine initial approximations provided by more robust but slower methods, such as bisection or the secant. The strategy:

  1. A few bisection steps trap the root in a small interval, on which g becomes a contraction.
  2. Successive approximations or Newton quickly finish the job.

For x3+12x−1=0 on [0,1], four bisection steps give the interval [0.0625,0.125], which contains ξ≈0.08329. You implement this in L5.

The generalization (Remark 7)

The result remains valid for g:M→M, g an α-contraction on M⊆R, M a closed set (for example all of R or [0,∞)). The estimate αn(b−a) no longer makes sense on an unbounded set, but this one remains:

∣xn​−ξ∣≤1−ααn​∣x0​−x1​∣,∀n∈N∗.

Example. g(x)=101+sinx​ on R: ∣g′(x)∣=10∣cosx∣​≤101​, so the equation 10x−1=sinx has exactly one solution on the whole real line.

Why all the hypotheses are needed

The missing hypothesisCounterexampleWhat breaks
g maps the interval into itselfg(x)=2x​+3 on [0,1]The fixed point, p=6, is outside the interval.
M closedg(x)=2x​ on (0,1]The sequence tends to 0, which is not in M: no fixed point.
A fixed, uniform α<1g(x)=x+x1​ on [1,∞)∣g(x)−g(y)∣<∣x−y∣, but always g(x)>x: no fixed point.
α<1g(x)=x2 on [0,1]Two fixed points (0 and 1): uniqueness is lost.
Continuity (Remark 3)g=1 on [0,21​], g=0 on (21​,1]The graph "jumps" over the diagonal: no fixed point.

A9 The lecture example, step by step intermediate

The problem. Compute with an error ≤10−4 the roots of the equation x3+12x−1=0.

  1. Isolating the roots. f(x)=x3+12x−1, f′(x)=3x2+12>0. By Rolle's sequence (P3), there is a single real root. Since f(0)=−1 and f(1)=12, ξ∈[0,1].
  2. The rewriting. Factor out x: x(x2+12)=1, so x=g(x), where g(x)=x2+121​.
  3. Computing α. g′(x)=−(x2+12)22x​. The source directly writes α=1692​; here is why. Let u(x)=(x2+12)22x​. Differentiating, u′(x)=(x2+12)32(12−3x2)​>0 on [0,1], so u is increasing and the maximum is at x=1: α=[0,1]sup​∣g′(x)∣=u(1)=1322​=1692​≈0.0118.
  4. Invariance. g is decreasing on [0,1], with g(0)=121​ and g(1)=131​. So g([0,1])=[131​,121​]⊂[0,1]. The source does not write this check, but the theorem requires it.
  5. The first iterations. With x0​=0: x1​=g(0)=121​ and x2​=g(x1​)=1441​+121​=1729144​≈0.08328.
  6. The number of iterations. From the estimate, with d(x0​,x1​)=∣x0​−x1​∣=121​ and 1−α=169167​: 121​⋅167169​(1692​)n<10−4⟺(1692​)n<169⋅104167⋅12​≈0.001186.
  7. Check the values. For n=1: 1692​≈0.0118>0.001186: not enough. For n=2: (1692​)2≈0.00014<0.001186: enough. So n=2.
  8. Conclusion. ξ≈x2​≈0.08328, with an accuracy better than 10−4. ∎
nxₙ|xₙ − xₙ₋₁|bound αⁿ|x₁−x₀|/(1−α)real error

The example, in the diagram

The curve is almost horizontal. That is why the sequence stops almost immediately.

Lecture: Newton and the tangent

Replace the curve with its tangent and see where it crosses the axis. The number of correct decimals nearly doubles with every step.

B1 The geometric idea and the formula beginner

Let f:[a,b]→R be of class C2([a,b]), with the equation f(x)=0 having a unique solution ξ∈[a,b]. It is hard to find where a curve crosses the axis, but very easy to find where a line does. So we replace the curve with the tangent.

Deriving the formula, in three lines

  1. The equation of the tangent at A(xn−1​,f(xn−1​)) is: y−f(xn−1​)=f′(xn−1​)(x−xn−1​).
  2. Set y=0 and x=xn​: −f(xn−1​)=f′(xn−1​)(xn​−xn−1​).
  3. Divide by f′(xn−1​)=0: xn​=xn−1​−f′(xn−1​)f(xn−1​)​,∀n∈N∗.​

The first computation: square root of 2, by hand

Let f(x)=x2−2, f′(x)=2x, x0​=2. The formula becomes:

xn​=xn−1​−2xn−1​xn−12​−2​=21​(xn−1​+xn−1​2​).
  • x1​=21​(2+1)=1.5
  • x2​=21​(1.5+1.3333)=1.41666…
  • x3​=1.4142156… (the exact value: 2​=1.4142135…)

In three steps we have five correct decimals. This is the ancient Babylonian (Heron's) method for extracting square roots.

The tangent lab

Press "Next step". The current tangent is drawn strongly, the old ones faded. The pink point on the axis is the next approximation.

B2 Newton's theorem: local convergence advanced

Theorem (Newton's method)

i) Under the above conditions, if in addition f′(ξ)=0, then there exists δ>0 such that, for every x0​∈[ξ−δ,ξ+δ], the sequence (xn​)n∈N∗​ given by xn​=xn−1​−f′(xn−1​)f(xn−1​)​ converges to ξ.

ii) If m1​,M2​ are given by m1​=infx∈[a,b]​∣f′(x)∣>0 and M2​=supx∈[a,b]​∣f′′(x)∣, then we have the estimates:

∣ξ−xn​∣≤2m1​M2​​(xn​−xn−1​)2,∀n∈N∗, ∣ξ−xn​∣≤2m1​M2​​(ξ−xn−1​)2,∀n∈N∗.

The word "local" is essential: the theorem guarantees convergence only close enough to the root.

Proof of part i): Newton is a fixed-point method

This is where the two chapters meet. Newton is also an iteration xn​=φ(xn−1​), with:

φ(x)=x−f′(x)f(x)​.
  1. Since f′ is continuous and f′(ξ)=0, f′ does not vanish in a neighborhood of ξ, so φ is well defined and of class C1 there.
  2. Differentiate: φ′(x)=1−f′(x)2f′(x)2−f(x)f′′(x)​=f′(x)2f(x)f′′(x)​.
  3. At the root, f(ξ)=0, so φ′(ξ)=0. This is the essence of the speed: the slope of the iteration is zero exactly at the root.
  4. By continuity, there is δ>0 with ∣φ′(x)∣≤21​ on I=[ξ−δ,ξ+δ]. So φ is a 21​-contraction on I (Remark 2).
  5. φ maps I into I: ∣φ(x)−ξ∣=∣φ(x)−φ(ξ)∣≤21​∣x−ξ∣≤δ.
  6. Apply the theorem from A5: for every x0​∈I, xn​→ the unique fixed point of φ in I, that is ξ. ∎

Proof of part ii)

We assume that the terms of the sequence stay in [a,b].

  1. The first inequality. Write Taylor around xn−1​, evaluated at xn​: f(xn​)=f(xn−1​)+f′(xn−1​)(xn​−xn−1​)+2f′′(c)​(xn​−xn−1​)2.
  2. From Newton's formula, f(xn−1​)+f′(xn−1​)(xn​−xn−1​)=0. What remains is f(xn​)=2f′′(c)​(xn​−xn−1​)2, so ∣f(xn​)∣≤2M2​​(xn​−xn−1​)2.
  3. From Lagrange, ∣f(xn​)∣=∣f(xn​)−f(ξ)∣=∣f′(d)∣⋅∣xn​−ξ∣≥m1​∣xn​−ξ∣.
  4. Combining: m1​∣ξ−xn​∣≤2M2​​(xn​−xn−1​)2, as required. ∎
  5. The second inequality. Write Taylor around xn−1​, evaluated at ξ: 0=f(ξ)=f(xn−1​)+f′(xn−1​)(ξ−xn−1​)+2f′′(c)​(ξ−xn−1​)2.
  6. Divide by f′(xn−1​) and use xn​=xn−1​−f′(xn−1​)f(xn−1​)​: we get ξ−xn​=−2f′(xn−1​)f′′(c)​(ξ−xn−1​)2. In absolute value, this gives the second estimate. ∎

B3 Quadratic convergence: digits double intermediate

The second estimate says that the new error is proportional to the square of the old error. Writing K=2m1​M2​​ and en​=∣ξ−xn​∣:

en​≤Ken−12​.

If en−1​≈10−3 and K≈1, then en​≈10−6, then 10−12. The number of correct decimals nearly doubles at each step. Here is Newton for 2​, computed with 130 digits (the correct decimals are marked in green):

Successive approximations

en​≤αen−1​
Linear convergence: you gain a fixed number of digits at each step.

Newton

en​≤Ken−12​
Quadratic convergence: you double the number of digits at each step.

The first estimate, with (xn​−xn−1​)2, is of great practical value, because ξ does not appear in it. You compute it directly and it gives you a stopping criterion with a guarantee:

2m1​M2​​(xn​−xn−1​)2≤ε⟹∣ξ−xn​∣≤ε.

B4 When Newton fails intermediate

The source names the main disadvantage: x0​ must be in [ξ−δ,ξ+δ], but neither ξ nor δ is known a priori. Here is what can happen, to watch live:

The gallery of failures

Choose each function from the list and press "Start". For arctan, move x₀ to either side of 1.39.

The situationExampleWhat happens
Cyclex3−2x+2, x0​=0x1​=1, x2​=0, x3​=1,… forever.
Overshootarctanx, x0​=1.5∣xn​∣ grows. The threshold is ∣x0​∣≈1.3917.
Moving away3x​, any x0​=0xn​=−2xn−1​: it doubles. f′(0) does not exist.

Horizontal tangentx3−x, near ±3​1​f′≈0: the next point jumps very far.

Basins of attraction: where you end up from each x0​

For f(x)=x3−x, with roots −1, 0, 1, each x0​ leads to a certain root. The next band colors the axis by destination. Near x≈0.447 (and symmetrically), the destination changes chaotically. Zoom in on that zone.

The message

The root Newton reaches is not necessarily the one closest to x0​. That is why we need a safe criterion for choosing x0​: the tangent theorem.

B5 The tangent theorem: choosing x₀ safely intermediate

Theorem (tangent method)

Let f:[a,b]→R be twice differentiable such that f(a)⋅f(b)<0, f′(x)=0 and f′′(x)=0, for every x∈[a,b]. Then the sequence given by x0​∈[a,b] with f(x0​)⋅f′′(x0​)>0,xn​=xn−1​−f′(xn−1​)f(xn−1​)​, ∀n∈N∗, converges strictly monotonically to ξ, the unique solution of the equation f(x)=0.

What each hypothesis says

The conditionMeaning
f(a)f(b)<0A root exists (the function changes sign).
f′=0f is strictly monotonic, so the root is unique. Tangents are not horizontal.
f′′=0The curve has constant concavity, it does not "twist".
f(x0​)f′′(x0​)>0We start on the side where the curve lies above the tangent, toward the root.

Derivatives cannot change sign without vanishing (Darboux's property). So f′ and f′′ have constant sign, and the graph falls into one of four cases.

The four cases

For each combination of signs, compare starting from a with starting from b.

SignsShapex0​The sequence
f′>0, f′′>0increasing, convexbdecreasing
f′>0, f′′<0increasing, concaveaincreasing
f′<0, f′′>0decreasing, convexaincreasing
f′<0, f′′<0decreasing, concavebdecreasing
The short rule

Choose the endpoint where f has the same sign as f′′. You do not need the table: compute f(a)f′′(a) and f(b)f′′(b) and take the positive one.

The proof (case f′>0, f′′>0)

The other cases reduce to this one, by replacing f with −f or x with −x.

  1. Uniqueness. f is strictly increasing and changes sign, so it has exactly one root ξ. The condition f(x0​)f′′(x0​)>0 with f′′>0 gives f(x0​)>0, so x0​>ξ.
  2. Induction. Suppose xn−1​>ξ. Then f(xn−1​)>0 and f′(xn−1​)>0, so xn​=xn−1​−f′(xn−1​)f(xn−1​)​<xn−1​: the sequence strictly decreases.
  3. It does not pass the root. From B2, xn​−ξ=2f′(xn−1​)f′′(c)​(ξ−xn−1​)2>0, so xn​>ξ. Thus ξ<xn​<xn−1​≤x0​ and we stay in [a,b].
  4. A limit exists. The sequence is decreasing and bounded below, so xn​→L∈[ξ,x0​].
  5. The limit is the root. f′ and f are continuous (f is twice differentiable). From f′(xn−1​)(xn−1​−xn​)=f(xn−1​), in the limit f′(L)⋅0=f(L), so f(L)=0 and L=ξ. ∎
Trap: f″ vanishes at an endpoint

For f(x)=x3+12x−1 on [0,1], f′′(x)=6x vanishes at 0, so the hypothesis "f′′=0 on [a,b]" is not satisfied on [0,1]. Solution: restrict the interval to [0.05,1], where f(0.05)<0, f(1)>0, f′′>0. The complete solution is in S3.

Monotonicity also gives you a test

If, under the conditions of the theorem, the sequence is not monotonic, you have a computation or hypothesis error. It is a quick check, useful in an exam.

B6 Comparing the methods intermediate

The race of the methods

The vertical axis shows the real error. The curvature of the Newton graph is the sign of quadratic convergence, while straight lines indicate linear convergence.

The last equation in the list shows a special case: g(x)=x1​+2x​ is exactly the Newton iteration for x2−2, so the two curves coincide.

BisectionSuccessive approximationsNewton / tangent
Formulac=2a+b​xn+1​=g(xn​)xn​=xn−1​−f′(xn−1​)f(xn−1​)​
Requiresa sign changea rewriting; g a contractionf′; f′=0; a good x0​
Speedlinear, factor 21​linear, factor αquadratic (simple root)
Guaranteealways, if f is continuousif the hypotheses are satisfiedlocal; global with the tangent theorem
Cost per stepone evaluation of fone evaluation of gone evaluation of f and one of f′
Error2n+1b−a​1−ααn​∣x1​−x0​∣2m1​M2​​(xn​−xn−1​)2
How to choose

If the derivative is easy to compute, use Newton with a correctly chosen x0​. If you do not have f′ or you already have a clear contraction, use successive approximations. If you know nothing, start with bisection and then refine.

Seminar

From recipes applied step by step to problems and proofs. Try on your own first, then open the solution.

S1 The worksheet and the checker beginner

Successive approximations
  1. Isolate the root: [a,b].
  2. Rewrite: x=g(x).
  3. α=sup∣g′∣<1?
  4. g([a,b])⊆[a,b]?
  5. Choose x0​, compute x1​.
  6. 1−ααn​∣x1​−x0​∣<ε: find n.
  7. Compute up to xn​.
Tangent method
  1. f(a)f(b)<0?
  2. f′=0 on [a,b]?
  3. f′′=0 on [a,b]?
  4. Choose the endpoint with f(x0​)f′′(x0​)>0.
  5. Compute m1​, M2​, K=2m1​M2​​.
  6. Iterate Newton.
  7. Stop when K(xn​−xn−1​)2≤ε.
The hypothesis checker

Enter your own function (for example exp(-x)-x or x^3-2x-5) and your own interval. Use it to check your solutions, not in place of reasoning.

The two roots

Choose the function from the list. The first one attracts toward 0, the second toward the negative root. The first one repels around the negative root, which is why a rewriting was needed.

The lesson

When you rewrite inversely, that is, use the inverse function, the slope is inverted: ∣G′(ξ)∣=∣g′(ξ)∣1​. An iteration that repels becomes one that attracts.

Problem 5. The lecture example, x3+12x−1=0, solved with the tangent, ε=10−4. Watch the hypotheses

On [0,1], f′′(x)=6x vanishes at 0: the hypothesis f′′=0 is not satisfied. We restrict: [0.05,1]. f(0.05)≈−0.3999<0, f(1)=12>0. f′(x)=3x2+12, m1​=f′(0.05)=12.0075. f′′(x)=6x>0, M2​=6; K≈0.25. x0​=1.

Level 3: argumentation

8. Let x0​>0, a>0. Show that Newton for f(x)=x1​−a computes a1​ without divisions. For which x0​ does it converge?

Solution

f′(x)=−x21​, so xn​=xn−1​+xn−12​(xn−1​1​−a)=xn−1​(2−axn−1​). Writing en​=1−axn​, we get en​=en−12​, so en​=e02n​. It converges exactly when ∣e0​∣<1, that is 0<x0​<a2​. Old processors performed division exactly this way.

9. Show that, if K∣ξ−x0​∣<1, the second estimate implies ∣ξ−xn​∣≤K1​(K∣ξ−x0​∣)2n. Apply it to 2​ with x0​=2 and ε=10−10.

Solution

Multiplying en​≤Ken−12​ by K: Ken​≤(Ken−1​)2. By induction, Ken​≤(Ke0​)2n. For 2​: K=21​, e0​=2−2​≈0.586, Ke0​≈0.293. The bound 2⋅0.2932n gives 5.8⋅10−9 for n=4 and 1.7⋅10−17 for n=5. So n=5 is guaranteed; in reality n=4 is already enough (the table in S3).

10. Let g be of class C2, with g(p)=p and g′(p)=0. Show that the iteration has, near p, quadratic convergence.

Solution

Taylor: xn+1​−p=g(xn​)−g(p)=g′(p)(xn​−p)+2g′′(c)​(xn​−p)2=2g′′(c)​(xn​−p)2. So en+1​≤2sup∣g′′∣​en2​. Newton is exactly this case (B2).

Level 4: top performance

11. Let f(x)=(x−ξ)mh(x), h(ξ)=0, m≥2. Show that φ′(ξ)=1−m1​. What do you conclude? How do you fix the method?

Solution

f′f​=mh+(x−ξ)h′(x−ξ)h​, so φ(x)=x−mh+(x−ξ)h′(x−ξ)h​. Dividing by x−ξ and passing to the limit: φ′(ξ)=1−m1​. Since φ′(ξ)=0, convergence is only linear, with factor 1−m1​ (for m=2, the factor is 21​). The fix: xn​=xn−1​−mf′(xn−1​)f(xn−1​)​ has φ′(ξ)=0 and restores quadratic convergence (L6).

12. Let g:[a,b]→[a,b] be continuous, with ∣g(x)−g(y)∣<∣x−y∣ for x=y, but no uniform α<1. Show that the fixed point exists and is unique, even though g is not a contraction. Example: sinx on [0,1].

Solution

Existence comes from Remark 3. Uniqueness: two fixed points would give ∣p1​−p2​∣<∣p1​−p2​∣, a contradiction. For sinx, p=0; x∣sinx∣​→1 near 0, so no α exists. The sequence still tends to 0, but very slowly: x1000​≈0.0546 when x0​=1. The theorem from the lecture cannot give a bound. On [1,∞), x+x1​ shows that the compact interval is essential.

13. Let f be of class C2, and gλ​(x)=x−λf(x). For which λ is gλ​ a contraction near the simple root ξ? Which λ is optimal and what method do you get?

Solution

gλ′​(ξ)=1−λf′(ξ). The condition ∣gλ′​(ξ)∣<1 means 0<λf′(ξ)<2. Optimal: λ=f′(ξ)1​, which cancels the slope. Replacing ξ with the current approximation, that is λn​=f′(xn−1​)1​, you get exactly Newton's method. So Newton appears as successive approximations with a parameter optimized at each step.

You write the methods and put them to the test. The JavaScript blocks run here, in the page. You can copy the Python and C++ programs, and below each one you see the output from actually running it.

L1 Setup beginner

You need no installation for the JavaScript blocks: type in the code box and press "Run". The function print(...) displays the result. An endless loop is stopped automatically after 4 seconds.

For Python: install Python 3 or use any online editor, save the code as lab.py and run python lab.py. For C++: g++ -std=c++17 methods.cpp -o methods, then run ./methods.

The rules of a correct implementation
  1. Limit the number of iterations (Remark 6).
  2. Check the denominator before dividing.
  3. Check that values stay finite.
  4. Also return the status (converged or not), not just a number.
  5. Do not ask for accuracy beyond the limit of the computation: in double precision, a relative ε≈10−15 is the ceiling.

Python: lab1_fixed_point.py
import math

def fixed_point(g, x0, eps=1e-6, nmax=100):
    """Method of successive approximations: x_(n+1) = g(x_n).
    Returns (approximation, iterations, history, status)."""
    x = x0
    history = [x0]
    for n in range(1, nmax + 1):
        try:
            x_new = g(x)
        except (ValueError, OverflowError, ZeroDivisionError):
            return x, n, history, "error: g cannot be evaluated"
        history.append(x_new)
        if not math.isfinite(x_new):
            return x_new, n, history, "divergent: non-finite value"
        if abs(x_new - x) <= eps:
            return x_new, n, history, "converged"
        x = x_new
    return x, nmax, history, "stopped: nmax reached"

# Lecture example: x^3 + 12x - 1 = 0, with g(x) = 1/(x^2 + 12)
x, n, hist, status = fixed_point(lambda x: 1 / (x**2 + 12), 0.0, 1e-4)
print(f"Lecture example: x = {x:.8f}, iterations = {n}, status = {status}")

# Bad rewriting of the same equation: x = x^3 + 13x - 1 (|g'| >= 13)
x, n, hist, status = fixed_point(lambda x: x**3 + 13*x - 1, 0.5, 1e-4, 50)
print(f"Bad rewriting: iterations = {n}, status = {status}")

Python: lab2_newton.py
def newton(f, df, x0, eps=1e-10, nmax=50):
    """Newton's method: x_n = x_(n-1) - f(x_(n-1)) / f'(x_(n-1))."""
    x = x0
    history = [x0]
    for n in range(1, nmax + 1):
        d = df(x)
        if d == 0:
            return x, n, history, "failed: f'(x) = 0"
        x_new = x - f(x) / d
        history.append(x_new)
        if abs(x_new) > 1e12:
            return x_new, n, history, "divergent"
        if abs(x_new - x) <= eps:
            return x_new, n, history, "converged"
        x = x_new
    return x, nmax, history, "stopped: nmax reached"

f  = lambda x: x**3 - x - 1
df = lambda x: 3*x**2 - 1
x, n, hist, status = newton(f, df, 2.0)
for k, v in enumerate(hist):
    print(f"x{k} = {v:.15f}")
print("status:", status, "| iterations:", n)

# A famous cycle: x^3 - 2x + 2, x0 = 0
_, n, hist, status = newton(lambda x: x**3 - 2*x + 2, lambda x: 3*x**2 - 2, 0.0, nmax=8)
print("Cycle:", hist[:6], "|", status)

C++: methods.cpp
#include <cmath>
#include <cstdio>
#include <functional>
using Fn = std::function<double(double)>;

struct Result { double x; int iterations; bool converged; };

Result fixedPoint(Fn g, double x0, double eps, int nmax) {
    double x = x0;
    for (int n = 1; n <= nmax; ++n) {
        double y = g(x);
        if (!std::isfinite(y)) return {y, n, false};
        if (std::fabs(y - x) <= eps) return {y, n, true};
        x = y;
    }
    return {x, nmax, false};
}

Result newton(Fn f, Fn df, double x0, double eps, int nmax) {
    double x = x0;
    for (int n = 1; n <= nmax; ++n) {
        double d = df(x);
        if (d == 0.0) return {x, n, false};
        double y = x - f(x) / d;
        if (!std::isfinite(y)) return {y, n, false};
        if (std::fabs(y - x) <= eps) return {y, n, true};
        x = y;
    }
    return {x, nmax, false};
}

int main() {
    auto a = fixedPoint([](double x) { return 1.0 / (x * x + 12.0); }, 0.0, 1e-4, 100);
    std::printf("Fixed point: x = %.8f, iterations = %d, converged = %d\n", a.x, a.iterations, a.converged);
    auto b = newton([](double x) { return x * x * x + 12.0 * x - 1.0; },
                    [](double x) { return 3.0 * x * x + 12.0; }, 1.0, 1e-10, 50);
    std::printf("Newton:      x = %.12f, iterations = %d, converged = %d\n", b.x, b.iterations, b.converged);
}

L4 The tangent method, with a guaranteed stop intermediate

Goal: the program chooses x0​ by itself and uses the estimate from the lecture.

Tangent method
Tasks
  1. Check the result against Problem 4 in S3.
  2. Solve x3+x−3=0 on [1,2] and ex+x−2=0 on [0,1].
  3. Add a monotonicity check. If the sequence is not monotonic, display a warning.
  4. Write a function that estimates m1​ and M2​ on a grid of points. Careful: a grid estimate is not a proof.
Python: lab3_tangent.py
import math

def choose_x0(f, d2f, a, b):
    """Choose the endpoint with f(x0) * f''(x0) > 0 (tangent method)."""
    if f(a) * f(b) >= 0:
        raise ValueError("We need f(a) * f(b) < 0")
    for c in (a, b):
        if f(c) * d2f(c) > 0:
            return c
    raise ValueError("Neither endpoint satisfies f(x0) * f''(x0) > 0")

def tangent(f, df, d2f, a, b, m1, M2, eps=1e-8, nmax=50):
    """Stops using the estimate from the lecture:
       |xi - x_n| <= M2 / (2*m1) * (x_n - x_(n-1))^2 <= eps"""
    x = choose_x0(f, d2f, a, b)
    K = M2 / (2 * m1)
    steps = [x]
    for n in range(1, nmax + 1):
        x_new = x - f(x) / df(x)
        steps.append(x_new)
        if K * (x_new - x)**2 <= eps:
            return x_new, n, steps
        x = x_new
    return x, nmax, steps

# ln x + x - 2 = 0 on [1, 2]: f' = 1/x + 1 >= 3/2, |f''| = 1/x^2 <= 1
x, n, steps = tangent(lambda x: math.log(x) + x - 2,
                      lambda x: 1/x + 1,
                      lambda x: -1/x**2,

L5 Refinement: bisection followed by Newton advanced

Goal: put Remark 1 into practice. You combine the robustness of bisection with the speed of Newton. At each step you keep an interval with a sign change; if the Newton step leaves the interval, you do bisection.

Safeguarded Newton

On arctanx, plain Newton from x0​=2 diverges, because 2>1.39. The safeguarded variant reaches the root.

Tasks
  1. Test on x3−2x+2 on [−3,0], where plain Newton can enter a cycle.
  2. Count how many evaluations of f and f′ you use and compare with pure bisection.
  3. Explain why the interval always contains a root, whatever steps are taken.
Python: lab4_hybrid.py
import math

def bisection(f, a, b, steps):
    """The initial approximation from Remark 1: a few halvings."""
    if f(a) * f(b) > 0:
        raise ValueError("f(a) and f(b) must have opposite signs")
    for _ in range(steps):
        c = (a + b) / 2
        if f(a) * f(c) <= 0:
            b = c
        else:
            a = c
    return a, b

def hybrid(f, df, a, b, eps=1e-12, nmax=100):
    """Safeguarded Newton: if the step leaves the interval or f' = 0,
    take a bisection step. The interval always brackets the root."""
    fa = f(a)
    if fa * f(b) > 0:
        raise ValueError("f(a) and f(b) must have opposite signs")
    x = (a + b) / 2
    newton_steps, bisection_steps = 0, 0
    for n in range(1, nmax + 1):
        fx = f(x)
        if fx == 0:
            return x, n, newton_steps, bisection_steps
        if fa * fx < 0:
            b = x
        else:
            a, fa = x, fx
        d = df(x)
        y = x - fx / d if d != 0 else a - 1
        if a < y < b:
            newton_steps += 1
        else:
            y = (a + b) / 2
            bisection_steps += 1
        if abs(y - x) <= eps:
            return y, n, newton_steps, bisection_steps
        x = y
    return x, nmax, newton_steps, bisection_steps

print("Bisection, 4 steps on [0, 1] for x^3 + 12x - 1:",
      bisection(lambda x: x**3 + 12*x - 1, 0, 1, 4))
# arctan x: plain Newton diverges from x0 = 2 (midpoint of [-3, 7]), the hybrid does not
print("Hybrid, arctan on [-3, 7]: x = %.2e, iterations = %d, Newton = %d, bisection = %d"
      % hybrid(math.atan, lambda x: 1/(1 + x*x), -3, 7))

L6 Measuring the order of convergence top performance

If en+1​≈Cenp​, then the order p can be estimated from three consecutive errors:

p≈ln(en​/en−1​)ln(en+1​/en​)​.
Estimate the order

Expected values: p≈1 for fixed point and multiple roots, p≈2 for Newton with a simple root. The first values may be far from the limit, and the last are affected by the finite precision of the computer.

Tasks
  1. For Newton on the double root, explain why en+1​/en​→21​.
  2. Try f(x)=(x−1)3, with m=1 and with m=3. What is the factor? Compare with problem 11 in S4.
  3. Find a function for which the Newton order is 3, that is f′′(ξ)=0. Hint: try sinx around 0.
Python: lab5_order.py
import math

def estimated_order(xs, root):
    """p_n = ln(e_(n+1)/e_n) / ln(e_n/e_(n-1))"""
    e = [abs(x - root) for x in xs]
    result = []
    for i in range(1, len(e) - 1):
        if e[i-1] > 0 and e[i] > 0 and e[i+1] > 1e-14:
            result.append(math.log(e[i+1]/e[i]) / math.log(e[i]/e[i-1]))
    return result

def fp_seq(g, x, n):
    v = [x]
    for _ in range(n):
        x = g(x); v.append(x)
    return v

def newton_seq(f, df, x, n, m=1):
    v = [x]
    for _ in range(n):
        d = df(x)
        if d == 0:
            break
        x = x - m * f(x) / d; v.append(x)
    return v

r = 0.7390851332151607
print("Fixed point, cos x:",
      [round(p, 3) for p in estimated_order(fp_seq(math.cos, 1.0, 12), r)][-3:])
print("Newton, cos x - x:",
      [round(p, 3) for p in estimated_order(newton_seq(lambda x: math.cos(x) - x, lambda x: -math.sin(x) - 1, 0.2, 5), r)])
f, df = (lambda x: (x-1)**2 * (x+2)), (lambda x: 2*(x-1)*(x+2) + (x-1)**2)
print("Newton, double root:",
      [round(p, 3) for p in estimated_order(newton_seq(f, df, 2.0, 12), 1.0)][-3:])
print("Modified Newton (m = 2), double root:",
      newton_seq(f, df, 2.0, 5, m=2)[:5])

L7 Real applications advanced

Kepler's equation: where is the planet?

The position on an elliptical orbit is obtained from Kepler's equation, E−esinE=M, where e is the eccentricity, M grows uniformly in time, and the unknown is E. There is no elementary formula for E.

The equation already has the form E=g(E), with g(E)=M+esinE and ∣g′(E)∣=e∣cosE∣≤e<1. The theorem applies on the whole axis, and α is exactly the eccentricity.

Orbit simulator

Raise the eccentricity toward 0.97 and watch how successive approximations need more and more iterations, while Newton stays stable.

Python: lab6_kepler.py
import math

def kepler_fp(M, e, eps=1e-12, nmax=100000):
    E = M
    for n in range(1, nmax + 1):
        new = M + e * math.sin(E)
        if abs(new - E) <= eps:
            return new, n
        E = new
    return E, nmax

def kepler_newton(M, e, eps=1e-12, nmax=50):
    E = M if e < 0.8 else math.pi
    for n in range(1, nmax + 1):
        new = E - (E - e*math.sin(E) - M) / (1 - e*math.cos(E))
        if abs(new - E) <= eps:
            return new, n
        E = new
    return E, nmax

print(f"{'e':>5} {'E (fixed point)':>16} {'iter':>6} {'E (Newton)':>16} {'iter':>5}")
for e in [0.0167, 0.2056, 0.5, 0.9, 0.967]:
    E1, n1 = kepler_fp(1.0, e)
    E2, n2 = kepler_newton(1.0, e)
    print(f"{e:5.4f} {E1:16.12f} {n1:6d} {E2:16.12f} {n2:5d}")

def irr(flows, r=0.1, eps=1e-10):
    """Internal rate of return: NPV(r) = sum CF_t / (1+r)^t = 0"""
    for _ in range(100):
        v = sum(c / (1+r)**t for t, c in enumerate(flows))
        d = sum(-t * c / (1+r)**(t+1) for t, c in enumerate(flows))
        new = r - v / d
        if abs(new - r) <= eps:
            return new
        r = new
    return r

print("IRR for [-1000, 300, 400, 500]: %.4f%%" % (100*irr([-1000, 300, 400, 500])))
    e  E (fixed point)   iter       E (Newton)  iter
0.0167   1.014179087165      6   1.014179087165     3
0.2056   1.190944767223     12   1.190944767223     4
0.5000   1.498701133518     10   1.498701133518     5
0.9000   1.862086686874     21   1.862086686875     6
0.9670   1.911436976490     25   1.911436976490     6

Eccentricities in the table: 0.0167 is Earth's orbit, 0.2056 Mercury's, 0.967 Halley's comet (approximate, rounded values). The number of steps does not increase strictly with e, because it also depends on the real slope ecosE at the solution, not just on the bound.

Internal rate of return

An investment of 1000 returns 300, 400 and 500 over the next three years. What annual interest rate r is equivalent? We have to solve the equation:

−1000+1+r300​+(1+r)2400​+(1+r)3500​=0.

The program above gives r≈8.90%. This is the equation that the IRR function in a spreadsheet solves.

L8 Accelerating convergence top performance

If the sequence converges linearly, xn+1​−p≈λ(xn​−p), two consecutive relations let you eliminate λ and estimate the limit directly. You get Aitken's Δ² formula:

x^n​=xn​−xn+2​−2xn+1​+xn​(xn+1​−xn​)2​.

If you restart the iteration from x^n​ you get Steffensen's method: quadratic convergence, without derivatives, using only g.

Python: lab7_aitken.py
import math

def steffensen(g, x, eps=1e-12, nmax=50):
    """Aitken acceleration applied repeatedly; uses no derivative."""
    for n in range(1, nmax + 1):
        x1 = g(x); x2 = g(x1)
        den = x2 - 2*x1 + x
        if den == 0:
            return x2, n
        new = x - (x1 - x)**2 / den
        if abs(new - x) <= eps:
            return new, n
        x = new
    return x, nmax

x = 1.0; n = 0
while abs(math.cos(x) - x) > 1e-12:
    x = math.cos(x); n += 1
print(f"Plain fixed point, g = cos: {x:.12f} in {n} iterations")
print("Steffensen, g = cos: %.12f in %d iterations" % steffensen(math.cos, 1.0))
Plain fixed point, g = cos: 0.739085133216 in 68 iterations
Steffensen, g = cos: 0.739085133215 in 5 iterations

From 68 iterations to 5. Each Steffensen iteration, however, uses two evaluations of g, so the fair comparison is 68 versus 10 evaluations.

Tasks
  1. Test Steffensen on g(x)=x4+x216​, the divergent rewriting from A7. What do you observe?
  2. Compare the number of evaluations with Newton, on the same equation.
What you should observe in task 1

Near the root, Steffensen can converge even when the simple iteration diverges, because it does not depend on the condition ∣g′(p)∣<1. However, convergence is no longer globally guaranteed, and it may fail from distant starting points.

L9 Beyond the real line and a mini-project top performance

Newton's formula also works for complex numbers. For z3−1=0 there are three roots. We color each starting point by the root it reaches. The boundary between the basins is a fractal, the same instability you saw on the real line in B4. This content goes beyond the source, which is limited to R; it is offered as an extension.

Z1 Review sheet beginner

Successive approximations

xn+1​=g(xn​)

Hypotheses: g:[a,b]→[a,b], ∣g′∣≤α<1.

Errors:
∣xn​−p∣≤αn(b−a)
∣xn​−p∣≤1−ααn​∣x0​−x1​∣

Geometry: the intersection with y=x.

Speed: linear.

Newton / tangent

xn​=xn−1​−f′(xn−1​)f(xn−1​)​

Hypotheses: f(a)f(b)<0; f′,f′′=0; f(x0​)f′′(x0​)>0.

Errors:
∣ξ−xn​∣≤2m1​M2​​(xn​−xn−1​)2
∣ξ−xn​∣≤2m1​M2​​(ξ−xn−1​)2

Geometry: the tangent crosses Ox at xn​.

Speed: quadratic, if f′(ξ)=0.

The most common mistakes

  • Checking ∣g′∣<1 but forgetting g([a,b])⊆[a,b].
  • Finding one solution and assuming it is the only one (exercise 3).
  • Checking α<1 at a single point, not on the whole interval.
  • Computing supg′ instead of sup∣g′∣.
  • Forgetting that the logarithm of α is negative and flips the inequality.
  • Starting the tangent method from the wrong endpoint.
  • Not noticing that f′′ vanishes on the interval.
  • Believing that a small step means a small error.
  • Working in degrees instead of radians.
